newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST-New Zealand business weeklies - Dec 6.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-New Zealand business weeklies - Dec 6.

text.p: THE NATIONAL BUSINESS REVIEW

Auckland Healthcare's planned $230 million project to relocate all high-tech functions to its central city site will make surplus beds available to private insurers. A private bed deal between the country's largest Crown health enterprise and Brierley Investments joint venture Aetna Health is already in the pipeline. This would give Aetna's policyholders the option of paying reduced premiums and having their treatment in spare Greenlane Hospital wards instead of a private hospital. The proposal flies in the face of Labour Party opposition to public hospital beds being contracted out to the private sector. Page

Telecom New Zealand is likely to be granted a licence before Christmas to operate in the soon-to-be-deregulated U.K. telecommunications market. But the company will not perform as a long-distance carrier in the U.K. It has applied for the licence in order to reduce costs of network traffic in Europe. Almost half the 46 organisations applying for licenses, including telecommunications giants MCI, Global One, Concert and AT&T, have applied to build their own telecommunications networks in the U.K. Page 8.

Cable operator Saturn Communications has warned it may pull the plug on hundreds of millions of dollars worth of cable roll-out if Independent Newspapers (INL) takes control of Sky Television. In a previously unreleased and hardhitting submission to the Commerce Commission, Petone-based Saturn says the Commerce Act will be breached if the purchase proceeds. Saturn, owned by US firm United International Holdings, is worried that if News Corporation-controlled INL is in charge of Sky, it may be denied access to crucial sports programming. Saturn is currently building a cable network in the Wellington

area and plans to have cable running past up to 600,000 homes within five to six years. But the company said the possible INL purchase could put the skids under expansion if the deal resulted in Saturn being shut out of the pay-TV market. Page 11.

More major alliances will follow Air New Zealand's commercial agreement with United Airlines this week as the airline moves toward becoming a globally competitive carrier. "We are not stopping with just this one but will go on into other theatres and markets and announce new agreements as they are negotiated," managing director Jim McCrea said. The United
code-share deal, to start in March, will give Air NZ two more US gateways -- San Francisco and Chicago -- while United gets Auckland-Sydney and possibly Brisbane. Page 13.

Whatever new government comes to power will face continuing pressure to limit state spending and check the soaring dollar from a powerful new lobby group it will find difficult to ignore. Thursday's historic exporters' economic summit in Wellington is certain to be only the first initiative of a group that represents close to half the country's GDP. It was the first time all major exporters and the tourism industry had

combined efforts to put pressure on the government to modify the hands-off policy in recent years. Participants made it clear the summit was not a one-off events and the newly created network would be maintained to keep up the pressure on the new government. Page 13.
THE INDEPENDENT BUSINESS WEEKLY

A controversial letter, connecting for the first time a former partner at law firm Russell McVeagh with offshore companies at the centre of allegedly fraudulent bloodstock deals in the late 1980s, has been tabled in evidence at the winebox Commission of Inquiry. Page 1.

Defrocked sharebroker Victor Ho is back in business as "Auckland's best financial services consultant". At least that's how he described on invitations to next Tuesday's opening of the NZ Money Centre. Ho is the centre's managing director. Its main product: the foreign exchange margins facility run by brokers
Ord Minnett. Page 1.

Mislabelled data have been used by ACT to mount an assault on government spending in a bid to get inflation down. The figures pop up in the first three paragraphs of a party task force report into the state of the rural economy. They show so-called "public sector inflation" burgeoning at a rate nine times greater than so-called "private sector inflation". But ACT MP Owen Jennings said the data were measures of non-tradeable and tradeable sector inflation rates -- not measures of private sector inflation and public section inflation rates, as claimed.
Page 1.

The Electricity Market Company (EMCO) will meet on Friday to consider an Economic Research Institute report into its own charging structure. This follows complaints from small electricity players that the present pricing system favours the big boys and is blocking competition. Since the wholesale electricity market opened on October 2, some small players have already opted out of the system. Others say they will follow unless the pricing mechanisms are changed to be more favourable to small participants. EMCO chief executive Lincoln Gould has

commissioned a ERI report and has set up a special working group of market participants which will meet on Friday to consider the report. However, the issue will not be easy to resolve, he says, because the two camps have diametrically opposing interests. Page 3.

As Air New Zealand this week announced a strategic commercial partnership with United Airlines, the world's largest airline, aviation analysts started to ponder the question -- where next? The Independent understands an agreement between Air NZ and United means before either party goes into another major

alliance with a third airline, they will consult with each other. Air NZ's spokesman David Beatson says the deal contains no veto rights on other alliances, nor any comprehensive requirements for the parties to get agreement on potential partners. Page 4.

Apple Fields plans to sell down its 43.8 percent holding in its offshoot, Dairy Brands. Apple Fields managing director Tom Kain told The Independent this week several options were open to the company, but its preference was to bring in a joint venture partner who would take on a portion of Apple Fields' holding.
Kain said Apple Fields had been working on the proposition "for some time" and was "having certain discussions". He refused to say who those discussions were with. Page 8.
